nameStory: This lichen gets its "mealy" name from its granular, powdery texture that looks just like coarse flour or cornmeal scattered on rocks. The "adhering" part refers to its impressive ability to stick tightly to whatever surface it's growing on - so firmly that it's hard to scrape off without damaging the rock underneath.
description: Adhering Mealy-lichen is a crusty lichen that forms rough, granular patches on rocks and sometimes grows right over mosses and other lichens. It looks like someone sprinkled coarse meal or sand across the stone surface, creating an irregular, bumpy coating. This lichen is relatively small, forming patches that can spread across several inches of rock surface. Like all lichens, it's actually two organisms living together - a fungus and an algae working as a team to survive in harsh conditions.

idTips.label: Granular texture
idTips.description: Run your finger over it - the surface feels rough and gritty like coarse sandpaper or cornmeal, quite different from smooth crusty lichens

idTips.label: Tight adherence
idTips.description: It sticks so firmly to rocks that it's very difficult to peel or scrape off - much more stubborn than loosely attached lichens

idTips.label: Rock preference
idTips.description: Almost always found growing directly on stone surfaces rather than on tree bark or soil

idTips.label: Overgrowth habit
idTips.description: Often grows right over mosses and other lichens like a crusty blanket, smothering what's underneath

idTips.label: Irregular patches
idTips.description: Forms scattered, uneven patches rather than neat circular colonies - the edges are typically ragged and bumpy

habitat: Look for this rare lichen on exposed rock surfaces, particularly in areas with some moisture but good air circulation. In New England, it would most likely be found on coastal rocks or inland stone outcrops where it can colonize both natural rock faces and old stone walls. Given its extreme rarity in our region, it may prefer specific rock chemistry or microclimates that haven't been fully documented yet.

seasonality.spring: Best time to spot this lichen as spring moisture brings out its granular texture more clearly and any reproductive structures become more visible.
seasonality.summer: Still identifiable but may appear more dried out and dusty during hot, dry periods. Look for it in shadier spots or areas that retain some moisture.
seasonality.fall: Good visibility as humidity increases and the lichen may appear more vibrant. Fall rains can make the granular texture more pronounced.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round since lichens don't die back seasonally. Snow cover may hide it temporarily, but it's actively photosynthesizing during mild winter days.

funFact: This lichen was originally discovered and named as one species, then scientists used DNA testing to realize it was actually completely different and moved it to an entirely new genus - it's like finding out your pet dog is actually a very convincing cat!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other crusty, granular lichens, but most similar species don't adhere nearly as tightly to their substrate. If you can easily scrape it off with a fingernail, it's probably not Adhering Mealy-lichen - this one really lives up to its "adhering" name.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents how modern DNA analysis is revolutionizing lichen classification - many lichens that look similar are turning out to be completely unrelated when scientists examine their genetics, leading to frequent name changes that can confuse field guides.
compareHints: Since this is the only Leprocaulon species documented in New England, compare it with other mealy or granular crusty lichens in the region. The key difference is its exceptional adherence to substrate - most granular lichens can be scraped off relatively easily, while this species bonds so tightly it seems almost fused to the rock. Its tendency to overgrow other lichens and mosses is also more aggressive than most similar species.
